lines.text: The estate agency sits on the high street between a solicitor's office and a coffee shop — a prime location for catching the eye of passing house-hunters. The window display features colour photographs of properties for sale, each with key details: price, number of bedrooms, and location. Inside, desks are arranged in an open-plan office where negotiators take calls, arrange viewings, and field enquiries from anxious buyers and impatient sellers. The branch manager oversees the team and handles valuations — visiting homes to assess their market value based on size, condition, location, and comparable recent sales. When a property is listed, the agency creates particulars: a detailed description with floor plans, photographs, and an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) rating. Viewings are arranged — sometimes accompanied by the agent, sometimes unaccompanied with a key safe code. Offers come in, and the negotiator's skill lies in managing expectations on both sides. Once a sale is agreed, the process moves to solicitors for conveyancing — the legal transfer of ownership. The entire process from listing to completion typically takes three to six months in England and Wales. Estate agents earn commission — usually 1–2% of the sale price — paid by the seller upon completion.

lines.text: Gazumping: the seller accepts a higher offer after already agreeing to sell to you. Gazundering: the buyer lowers their offer just before exchange. Both are legal in England and Wales (not in Scotland, where the system differs) and deeply unpopular.
lines.name: Gazumping: the seller accepts a higher offer after already agreeing to sell to you. Gazundering: the buyer lowers their offer just before exchange. Both are legal in England and Wales (not in Scotland, where the system differs) and deeply unpopular.

lines.text: In Scotland, property sales work differently — offers are legally binding once accepted, eliminating gazumping. Properties are often sold through a 'closing date' (sealed-bid deadline). Scottish solicitors handle both legal work and sales, unlike the separate estate-agent model in England.
lines.name: In Scotland, property sales work differently — offers are legally binding once accepted, eliminating gazumping. Properties are often sold through a 'closing date' (sealed-bid deadline).
